walkthroughs.body_html:
Experimental Techniques & Analysis — a core area of GCSE Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Experimental Techniques & Analysis brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Experimental Techniques & Analysis.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Limewater turns cloudy in the presence of:
If a reaction has a negative Gibbs free energy change, what does that mean?
options: The reaction is thermodynamically feasible — it can proceed — but it may still be very slow.
Water molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen gas when they boil.
A reaction with negative delta G will always happen quickly.
A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.

mcqs.q: When water boils, what is broken?
options: Intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) between water molecules are broken — the O-H covalent bonds stay intact.
A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.
Water molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen gas when they boil.
The covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen atoms are broken when water boils.

mcqs.q: What does a mole of a substance represent?
options: A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.
Avogadro's number (6.02 x 10^23) of particles of that substance.
A mole is a unit of mass equal to the relative molecular mass in grams of any substance.
A mole is a unit of volume equal to 24 dm^3 at any temperature.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Test for CO₂”?
options: Useful mixture made to a precise formula, e.g. paints, medicines, fuels.
Single element or compound — a sharp melting/boiling point shows purity.
